title: Meta publishes six Muse Spark math papers, five resolve long-open problems
subtitle: Mathematicians used the standard Meta.ai chat interface — no custom scaffold, no proof harness — and co-authored papers answering questions open for up to a decade.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: On October 2, Meta posted six research-level mathematics papers co-authored by Muse Spark 1.1 and 1.2 and human mathematicians, with Meta claiming that five of the six resolve previously open problems. The problems span probability (a sharp threshold for fitting random Gaussian points to ellipsoids), differential equations (finite-time blow-up for the mass-critical biharmonic nonlinear Schrödinger equation, open since 2015), group theory (a counterexample showing semiabelian groups need not be monomial), optimization (exactness of a cycle-based relaxation), arithmetic physics, and non-associative algebra (disproof of a conjecture about solvable evolution algebras).

Meta's methodology note is the news, more than any single result. The papers used the regular Meta.ai chat interface in Thinking Mode — no custom research scaffold, no specialized proof-checking harness, no fine-tuning aimed at the target problems. Human mathematicians chose the problems, steered the sessions, corrected drafts, and had other mathematicians review the arguments. The system did not pick its own research agenda or independently validate results. That framing is deliberate: Meta is positioning Muse Spark as a strong general collaborator, not an autonomous proof-generating system.

Context matters here. OpenAI's August 2026 'ten open math problems' Lean-formalized claims drew pushback over credit attribution, and Google DeepMind's Argon release has faced benchmaxxing accusations in Bloomberg. Meta publishing worked-through papers — with named human co-authors willing to defend the proofs — is a different kind of claim, and reviewers in the community will replicate against transcripts rather than against leaderboards. Expect the next few weeks to produce either confirmed novel contributions or specific objections to specific lemmas.

A takeaway for learners: the Muse Spark papers are a chance to see what AI-assisted research actually looks like when the AI is a chat window and not a bespoke pipeline. Read one of the preprints alongside its transcript. Note where the model proposed a line of attack, where the human corrected it, and where a reviewer later strengthened a lemma. That workflow is likely to become the template for AI-aided science long before fully autonomous systems arrive.
